Lessons.Title: Outliers
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: identify a possible outlier with a specified rule, determine its impact on center and variability, investigate whether it is a legitimate observation or a data error, and justify a decision to retain or exclude it. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 14, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/14/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Source roles: Building On HSS-ID.A.1; Addressing HSS-ID.A.1, HSS-ID.A.2, HSS-ID.A.3; Building Towards HSS-ID.A.3.

Original hypothetical dataset of six service times (minutes): 9,10,11,12,13,100. Median is (11+12)/2=11.5; with halves 9,10,11 and 12,13,100, Q1=10 and Q3=13; IQR=3. The upper 1.5-IQR fence is 13+1.5×3=17.5 minutes, so 100 is an outlier by that rule. The lower fence is 10−4.5=5.5.

With all six observations, mean=(9+10+11+12+13+100)/6=155/6≈25.83 minutes. Without 100, the remaining five have mean 11 and median 11 minutes. Removing the observation changes the represented population and requires a defensible cause, not just a prettier statistic.

Investigate whether 100 resulted from a unit or transcription error, an exceptional but genuine event, or a different process. If the cause is unknown, present results with and without it and disclose the decision; never silently remove data. The source uses contextual data and statistical technology, not a mandate to discard all distant points.

Student activity: reproduce the box plot, show both 1.5-IQR fences, compare mean and median with/without the suspected outlier, propose a verification procedure, and write a justified reporting recommendation. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for accurate quartiles/fences, correct changes in center, defensible source investigation, and transparent reporting (max 8).

Source-activity A/B review, IM Algebra 1 First Edition U01:L14: Investigate an outlier before deleting; distinguish error from valid extreme. Keep original first-party mathematical material and graphics; source artwork identity is NOT claimed. All physical/technology/partner work remains NOT_PERFORMED unless observed.

EDULYTIKS_AUTHORED_COOLDOWN (PUBLISHER_COOLDOWN_UNVERIFIED): Find fences 5.5 and17.5 for 9,10,11,12,13,100; explain why 100 is outlying but not automatically discarded. A teacher scores 0, 1 or 2 per criterion: Quartile and fence; Mean vs median; Reasoned retain/exclude choice. Total 6. No publisher protected Cool-down is claimed as read or reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Outlier
KeyConcepts.Definition: An unusual observation that differs substantially from the bulk of data.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A formal 1.5×IQR fence is one possible diagnostic, not a compulsory deletion rule.
KeyConcepts.Example: For Q3=13 and IQR=3, values above 17.5 are flagged.

KeyConcepts.Title: Influence on center
KeyConcepts.Definition: A large extreme affects the mean more than the order-based median.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compute the relevant statistics with and without a disputed value.
KeyConcepts.Example: Adding 100 changes mean 11 to about 25.83 in a six-value dataset.

KeyConcepts.Title: Responsible exclusion
KeyConcepts.Definition: An observation must be investigated before excluding it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check data entry, units and whether it belongs to the intended population.
KeyConcepts.Example: If 100 is real, report both the value and its effect.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute outlier fences
WorkedExamples.Question: For 9,10,11,12,13,100, use median-of-halves and 1.5×IQR.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a first-party dataset and show independently checkable reasoning.
Steps: Since 100>17.5, it is flagged by this diagnostic.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 100 minutes is an upper outlier by the 1.5-IQR rule.
WorkedExamples.Check: 100 lies above 17.5; no other listed observation lies beyond either fence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare means before and after
WorkedExamples.Question: How does the 100-minute value influence the mean?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a first-party dataset and show independently checkable reasoning.
Steps: Without 100 the sum is 55 over five values, mean 11.
The mean falls by about 14.83 minutes when excluding that observation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Investigate an unexpected value
WorkedExamples.Question: An observation of 100 minutes might be a transcription error from 10 minutes. Should it be automatically removed?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a first-party dataset and show independently checkable reasoning.
Steps: Verify the original recording and the units.
Ask whether the event legitimately belongs to the defined population.
If a confirmed entry error, correct it with a documented source record.
If valid, retain it or report sensitivity analyses with stated rationale.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No automatic deletion: investigate provenance and report the decision.
WorkedExamples.Check: A numerical fence flags an observation; it does not establish the cause.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Removing every flagged value without investigation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Extreme observations can be true and important.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify source and report transparent sensitivity analyses.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the mean before and after with the same denominator
Claiming a quartile rule guarantees a data error
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Outlier fences are statistical diagnostics, not truth tests.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separately assess record quality and sampling context.

SummaryPoints: One 1.5-IQR fence is Q3+1.5×IQR; diagnose, do not automatically delete.
In the original example, 100 exceeds the upper fence 17.5 minutes.
Mean 25.83 with versus 11 without the extreme illustrates influence.
Teacher must judge the defensibility of excluding values; no fabricated research or source checks.
